fact.thing: share of a crypto capital gain that is taxable
fact.claim: If the CRA treats your crypto sales as capital, you add half of the gain to your income. If it treats your trading as a business, you report the full profit, so twice as much of it gets taxed. The CRA looks at things like how often you buy and sell, how long you hold, what you know about crypto markets, how much time you spend on it, and whether you trade with borrowed money. No single factor settles it, and these factors only suggest a business. The CRA decides each case on its facts.

plain.what: Canada's tax office, the CRA, looks at how you handle bitcoin — digital money you hold online, not through a bank. If it calls your sales capital, you add only half of your profit to your income. If it calls your trading a business, you add the whole profit, so twice as much gets taxed.
plain.so_what: On a $10,000 profit, one label adds $5,000 to your income and the other adds all $10,000 — same profit, your share of tax can be twice as big.
plain.do: Write down how often you trade, how long you hold, and whether you use borrowed money.
